source.title: Towards Principled Evaluations of Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability and Control
source.authors: Aleksandar Makelov; George Lange; Neel Nanda

page_placements.theme: Fixed-size fragmentation and duplication: one concept spread over several latents of one SAE

record.tranche_reason: The study reports SAE over-splitting and investigates whether the SAE objective can favor many-feature solutions over a two-feature solution, refining the interpretation of splitting.
record.gate_note: The study does not compare smaller and larger dictionaries for coarse-to-fine feature matches, input coverage, or direction similarity. It also does not test Matryoshka SAEs. Other SAE controllability, reconstruction, and interpretability results do not directly measure the claim's size-related splitting pattern.
record.test_reason: The toy-model analysis (Appendix A.15, Fig. 14) argues the ℓ2+λℓ1 SAE objective itself prefers many-feature solutions over the ideal two-feature solution for a two-cluster distribution. That bears on V6: splitting can be produced by the objective rather than by the model's units. The GPT-2 Small over-splitting of Pos is observed at a single dictionary size, with no cross-size matching. So it does not test V1–V5.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors report that task-specific SAEs over-split the binary Pos attribute into many less interpretable features. They show in a toy Gaussian-mixture model that a many-feature SAE can achieve lower loss than the ideal two-feature SAE for any λ, even with infinite data, suggesting over-splitting may generalize. They add that over-splitting need not mean SAE failure, since the binary attribute may not be part of an optimal sparse description.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains SAEs on IOI activations and studies over-splitting and toy-model loss preferences; it does not run the claim's same-activations dictionary-size sweep or evaluate cross-size feature matching.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that over-splitting is similar above chance across random seeds and training datasets. The toy comparison varies the L1 regularization coefficient λ.

fits_no_version.finding: Task SAEs on GPT-2 Small L10H0 queries split the binary Pos attribute into ≥10 features. These fire on small, mostly non-overlapping subsets with no clear meaning, whereas a single supervised Pos feature suffices for editing.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAEs can over-split a binary model attribute into many uninterpretable features at a fixed dictionary size.

fits_no_version.finding: Feature occlusion: across dictionary sizes 1024–8192 and a wide λ range, task SAEs find IO-name features but never more than 22 S-name features (Fig. 6 left). Reducing IO feature norm raises the S-feature count.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAEs preferentially learn features for higher-magnitude attributes, occluding lower-magnitude ones regardless of dictionary size.

record.problems: The claim-relevant real-model observation is qualitative and limited to one model and task. The objective-preference comparison is a toy-model analysis with approximate loss estimates; the paper does not compare alternative objectives such as Matryoshka SAEs.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant reported results left out.

untested.parts: No dictionary-size sweep for splitting, parent–child matching, input coverage or direction proximity.
No large-model or open-SAE-release test of size-driven splitting.
No nested families or concept hierarchy.
No parent/child firing or absorption test.
No cross-size latent decomposition or novel-latent test.
No Matryoshka or alternative objective. No hierarchical or correlated inputs. No demonstration that the GPT-2 Pos split is objective-caused rather than reflecting model units.

missing.what: Robustness check: Pos features from different seeds and from different training datasets are similar above chance. The authors take this to mean over-splitting is not solely overfitting. No numbers are given.
Control: a 2-feature SAE trained on the toy mixture reliably recovers the ideal ±μ solution for 1≤λ≤3.

record.verdict_notes: Main contribution is a supervised-dictionary evaluation framework for IOI. Over-splitting is a secondary qualitative finding. V6 support is limited to a non-hierarchical toy and to a randomized-construction loss bound, not to trained-SAE losses.

versions.untested_parts: No smaller-versus-larger dictionary comparison, parent-to-child feature matching, direction proximity, or coverage of a coarse feature's inputs.
No large-model or open-SAE-release test of the specified size-related splitting pattern.
No test of nested feature families or a hierarchy of concepts.
No parent-child firing or sparsity-change test of absorption.
No decomposition of larger-SAE latents into smaller-SAE latents or test for novel latents.

The toy-model result tests whether the SAE objective can prefer over-splitting in a two-component Gaussian mixture, but does not test Matryoshka SAEs or establish that splitting in the GPT-2 Small task SAE is caused by the objective rather than reflecting model units.

rows.subject: GPT2-Small
rows.operation_detail: Measured feature splitting in task-specific SAE activations.
rows.measure: Number and activation pattern of features for the binary Pos attribute
rows.value: Pos was split into many features (e.g. ≥ 10) that activate on small, mostly non-overlapping subsets of examples with the same Pos value and have no clear semantic interpretation.
rows.note: This is evidence of task-SAE over-splitting, but it does not compare dictionary sizes or show a coarse feature being replaced by nearby child directions that jointly cover its inputs.
rows.check: Correct to leave unlinked. There is one dictionary size (1024, 16×) and no parent feature, coverage or direction comparison, so it cannot show V1's size-driven splitting. On its own it cannot attribute the split to the objective (V6): the authors note Pos may not belong to an optimal sparse description. Value is qualitative ('e.g. ≥ 10' features).

conditions.value: Uniform mixture of two standard multivariate Gaussians ±μ + N(0, I_d)
Sweep; plotted range is cut off near λ ≈ 7
Infinite-data loss estimated empirically for the comparison

rows.baseline: Idealized SAE with two features, one for each mixture component
rows.value: The randomized many-feature construction gives a lower total-loss upper bound than the ideal two-feature solution in the reported comparison; trained SAEs reliably learned solutions with many active features across λ values.
rows.note: Authors describe the comparison as empirical evidence and an approximate upper bound; the text does not provide exact plotted loss values.
rows.check: The many-feature comparator is a randomized construction (m=1,000, γ≈2.35, β tuned), not a trained SAE. It gives an approximate upper bound on infinite-data loss, so 'lower loss' is shown only for that construction. The trained many-feature SAEs are described only qualitatively, with no loss or feature counts. Baseline: the 2-feature SAE does recover the ideal solution for 1≤λ≤3. The data are a two-cluster mixture, not correlated or hierarchical features, and no plotted values are given.

relation.reason: Its own results (toy loss comparison, trained toy SAEs, Pos over-splitting) bear on V6.

tranche.reason: The toy-model argument (A.15) says the l2+lambda*l1 objective itself prefers many-feature solutions for one binary variable. That bears on whether splitting reflects model units (V6).

source_check.notes: Shares an author (Neel Nanda) with an original, so this is not an independent test. The V6 evidence is a randomized construction with an approximate infinite-data loss read from a figure, plus a qualitative note on trained SAEs. The toy has no hierarchy or correlation.

statements.correction: Randomized m=1,000 construction gives a lower approximate infinite-data total loss than the ideal 2-feature SAE (Fig. 14, figure-only). Trained many-feature SAEs reliably learn many active features (stated without numbers). No uncertainty is given for the toy.
statements.problem: Numbers match (d=100, ||mu||2=2, m=1,000, 1<=lambda<=3 for the 2-feature SAE). Caveat: 'reports uncertainty' holds study-wide (margin of error, statistical significance in the editing tests), but the Fig. 14 toy result has no uncertainty.

statements.correction: Over-splitting of one binary variable: two-component Gaussian mixture (toy, A.15) and the Pos attribute (GPT-2 Small L10H0 queries, Sec. 6.2).
statements.problem: none; the two-Gaussian toy has no correlation or hierarchy between features. The real-data over-splitting (Pos in GPT-2 Small) is also a single binary attribute.

statements.correction: Randomized many-feature construction beats the ideal 2-feature solution across the plotted lambda range (0 to ~7). A trained 2-feature SAE recovers +-mu for 1<=lambda<=3.
statements.problem: none; the plotted sweep runs from 0 to about 7, and the text says such constructions exist for any lambda. The many-feature curve is the randomized construction.

statements.correction: Pos is split into many (e.g. >=10) task-SAE features. They fire on small, mostly non-overlapping subsets with no clear meaning. Supervised dictionaries edit Pos by replacing 1 active feature (Sec. 4).

Dictionary sizes 1024-8192 (Fig. 6), effective l1 over two orders of magnitude. S features with F1>0.5 never exceed 22; IO features often match the number of names. Subtracting a fraction alpha of IO features (size 1024, l1 0.2) raises the S-feature count (Fig. 6 right, A.14).
statements.problem: Minor: the 22 counts S features with F1>0.5. Fig. 6 shows dictionary sizes 1024-8192 and effective l1 over two orders of magnitude.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The many-feature SAE construction has lower total loss than the idealized two-feature solution in the reported comparison, and trained SAEs reliably learn many-feature solutions; this supports an objective-driven over-splitting mechanism in this toy setting (r2).
